task.goal: Help a household share one bicycle without last-minute conflicts.
hard_constraints: Three adults use one bike and a paper calendar; no tracking app.
Keep personal trip destinations private and allow emergency use.
Compare missed trips, idle time and coordination effort for two weeks.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reserve only the time you need
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the paper calendar as the sole booking record. Each adult writes an initial and departure–return window as soon as a trip becomes likely; destinations and purposes stay private. The first entry holds the bike. Overlapping requests require an agreed swap before either person relies on the bike. Release cancelled bookings promptly, and keep the key in one agreed place whenever the bike is home. Allow a realistic return buffer.

This changes the outcome by exposing conflicts early while leaving unbooked hours available to everyone. It requires people to check the calendar and return on time; uncertain schedules and habitual early booking could undermine it. No materials beyond the calendar, a writing implement and existing key are needed.

An emergency overrides an ordinary booking when the bike is home: tell the affected adult if reachable, mark an estimated return, and disclose no destination. A bike already away cannot be recalled reliably with these resources.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare seven days of the current routine with seven days of reservations, matching weekdays. On the calendar, tally intended trips missed because the bike was unavailable, approximate daylight hours the bike sat unused, and minutes spent checking, discussing or recording arrangements. Include measurement effort consistently in both weeks. Also mark booked windows that went unused. The mechanism is doubtful if missed trips do not fall, or if unused reservations and coordination effort rise substantially. Two weeks provide a preliminary comparison; different trip demand or emergencies could explain differences.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Rotate predictable priority periods
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Divide each day into morning, afternoon and evening periods on the calendar. Assign priority to the three adults in a repeating rotation, shifting the starting adult each day. The priority adult marks whether they need their period by the preceding evening; otherwise it becomes open. Another adult may reserve a released period by initialling it. Trips must finish before the next claimed period, including a return buffer. Keep the key in a fixed place when the bike is home.

Predictable ownership reduces repeated negotiation and distributes desirable periods across people. Only initials and times appear, keeping destinations private. Implementation needs one initial calendar setup and brief daily checks. It assumes most trips fit the periods and that adults can sometimes shift departure times. Long or inflexible trips require an explicit swap, and unequal demand may make equal priority inefficient.

Emergency use takes precedence whenever the bike is present, with notice to the displaced adult where possible and an estimated return on the calendar. It cannot guarantee access while someone is riding.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use the current routine for week one and rotating priority for week two. Record daily missed intended trips caused by bike availability, approximate unused daylight hours, and coordination minutes. Mark whether each missed trip fell inside someone else's claimed but unused period. Before starting, agree what increase in effort or idle time would outweigh fewer missed trips. Reject or revise the routine if rigid periods themselves cause repeated misses or claimed periods sit empty. Compare matching weekdays, while noting that a single week per condition cannot establish a reliable causal effect.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Allocate conflicts by fewest recent rides
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Each evening, adults enter only their next day's desired departure–return windows and initials on the calendar. Nonoverlapping requests stand automatically. For an overlap, priority goes to whoever has completed the fewest bike trips during the preceding seven days, counted from small completion ticks on the calendar. Break ties using a rotating initial order written at the top. Resolve conflicts that evening; later requests fit around confirmed windows unless everyone affected agrees to change them. Cancel unused requests promptly and return the key to its agreed place.

The mechanism gives a clear, inspectable answer to competing requests while compensating people who have used the shared bike less. It needs a short evening check and one tick per completed outing, without recording destinations. It assumes ride counts are an acceptable fairness measure: a short outing and a long outing count equally, so this may fit poorly where needs differ sharply. It also exposes usage frequency, although personal destinations remain private.

An emergency overrides the allocation when the bike is home, without requiring disclosure of its purpose. Notify displaced users if possible and mark the expected return. Emergency rides also receive completion ticks.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare one week of the current routine with one week using the rule. Tally bike-related missed intended trips, approximate unused daylight hours and coordination minutes on the calendar. Inspect each contested window: was the decision settled the evening before, and did the winner actually use it? The rule fails its basic purpose if conflicts still require last-minute bargaining, or if fewer rides merely redistribute missed trips without an acceptable fairness benefit. Ask each adult privately whether the allocation felt workable; two weeks cannot establish longer-term fairness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Fit flexible trips around fixed ones
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a brief evening scheduling check to fit the next day's trips together. Each adult writes only initials, expected bike-use duration including a return buffer, and earliest departure/latest return. Someone with a fixed appointment can give a narrow window without explaining why. No destinations or purposes are recorded.

Together, place the least flexible trips first, then fit flexible trips into the remaining gaps. Confirm actual departure–return times on the calendar before ending the check. Entry order gives no priority. If two trips cannot both fit, ask whether either person can shift; if neither can, use a rotating tie-break initial and acknowledge the unresolved missed trip in advance. Late requests use remaining gaps or require agreement from affected adults.

The working principle is to use scheduling flexibility to preserve trips that would otherwise collide. This differs from awarding an overlap to the first claimant: a flexible request can move so both people ride. It assumes adults know roughly how long they need and that some trips can shift. If everyone's timing is fixed, this routine offers little benefit and may add discussion.

Implementation needs the existing calendar, key, an available pen, and a short shared check. Keep the key in one agreed place when home and cross out cancelled allocations. An emergency may override the schedule whenever the bike is present, without disclosing its destination or purpose; mark an expected return and notify displaced users if reachable. Access cannot be guaranteed while someone is riding.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
For seven days, retain the current routine; for the next seven, use flexible-window scheduling. In both weeks, tally daily intended trips missed because the bike was unavailable, approximate hours the bike was home and unused within the same agreed daily observation period, and total person-minutes spent coordinating and recording measurements. Compare matching weekdays and note total requested trips.

During the trial week, mark each occasion when shifting a flexible trip allowed both requests to happen. Inspect after three days: if no requests can shift and discussion takes longer, the proposed mechanism has little support. After two weeks, judge whether fewer misses justify any added effort or idle time. This is a preliminary comparison; changing demand and emergencies can explain differences.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use a waiting queue with bounded loans
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the calendar as a same-day waiting queue rather than allocating future time slots. An adult who wants the bike writes their initial and latest useful departure time, without a destination or purpose. Cross out requests that expire or are withdrawn. When the bike returns, the earliest still-active entry gets the next turn; skip anyone who is not ready to leave. With no waiting entries, anyone may take it.

Agree on a normal maximum loan length that accommodates common local trips. Before leaving, the borrower checks the queue and writes an expected return. If someone is waiting, the borrower must return within that limit. A longer outing requires agreement from those already waiting. Return the key to one agreed place and tell the next waiting adult that the bike is back when practical.

The mechanism is a work-conserving queue: the bike keeps moving between ready users, while bounded loans stop one discretionary outing from blocking several others. It could suit a household whose trips are mostly short and whose departure times tolerate some waiting. It assumes adults can check the calendar, communicate at home, and honor return estimates. Fixed appointments, long essential trips, and requests entered while the bike is already away remain weaknesses. Implementation needs only calendar space, an existing writing implement, the key, and a brief agreement on the loan limit.

An emergency goes ahead of the queue whenever the bike is home. Mark an expected return and notify displaced adults if reachable; no explanation or destination is required. Emergency access cannot be guaranteed while the bike is away.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Keep the current routine for seven days, then try the queue for seven. In both weeks, tally bike-related missed intended trips, approximate home-and-unused hours during the same daily observation period, and total person-minutes spent coordinating and recording. Count trips abandoned because the loan limit was too short as missed trips. Compare matching weekdays and note demand and emergencies. Inspect the first three contested returns: did the next ready adult actually get the bike promptly? Repeated empty handoffs, excessive checking, or more missed trips would undermine the mechanism. The two-week comparison is preliminary because demand may differ.

EXPAND.title: Use short renewable checkouts with a waiting queue
EXPAND.proposal:
Replace advance reservations with bounded borrowing: someone may take the bike when it is home, but a waiting adult gets the next turn at the agreed return time. This targets a weakness of advance reservations: a tentative booking can block another person even when the bike is idle.

Before starting, the three adults choose a checkout limit that accommodates their usual short outings, such as 60 minutes. On departure, write only an initial and promised return time on the paper calendar. Someone wanting the bike while it is away writes their initial in a waiting queue. On return, the rider leaves the key in its agreed place and offers the bike to the first waiting adult. A waiting adult who no longer needs it crosses out their initial. Renewals are allowed only when nobody is waiting; check the calendar before renewing. A longer outing requires agreement from both other adults before departure. If they cannot agree, that outing cannot rely on the bike.

Emergency use moves ahead of the queue whenever the bike is home. Mark an estimated return and notify anyone displaced if reachable; no destination or explanation is required. An overdue rider returns the bike and key as soon as possible; the next waiting person then takes priority. These resources cannot recall a bike already away.

The mechanism keeps access moving through actual demand rather than speculative claims. It requires predictable short trips, reliable returns, an existing writing implement, and willingness to accept waiting. It provides less certainty for future appointments and may exclude useful long rides.
EXPAND.experiment:
One adult volunteers to maintain the two-week tally. Use the prior first-entry reservation routine for seven days, then renewable checkouts for seven days. Compare matching weekdays: count intended trips missed because access or the checkout limit prevented them, estimate bike idle time during the same daily observation window, and record everyone's coordination minutes, including measurement. Separately tally waiting minutes and long outings abandoned or split.

Stop the checkout trial early if a missed promised return causes another adult to miss a time-critical trip; restore reservations and retain the observations. Otherwise, keep it only if fewer missed trips justify any increased waiting or coordination, using a tolerance agreed before starting. Equal or worse missed trips, or idle time merely converted into waiting, would show no improvement over reservations. Two weeks give a preliminary comparison because demand may differ.

EXPAND.title: Reduce competing departures through private trip consolidation
EXPAND.proposal:
Reduce the number of separate bike requests before allocating access. Each evening, every adult privately considers whether their next day's flexible outings could be combined into one bike outing, postponed, or completed without the shared bike. Nobody reports destinations, purposes, or rejected options. Consolidation is voluntary: essential or time-sensitive trips remain unchanged.

Each person marks only their resulting departure–return window and initial on the calendar. At a brief evening check, resolve overlaps by asking whether either person can move their whole outing. If both can move, alternate who moves using a single initial on the calendar; if neither can move, alternate who receives the bike and record the other trip as missed. Later requests use remaining gaps unless affected adults agree to a change. Cross out cancellations promptly. On return, leave the key in one agreed place; if delayed, alert the next user when an existing means of contact is available. Do not assume another device is available.

Emergency use overrides ordinary arrangements when the bike is home, with an estimated return on the calendar and notice to displaced adults if reachable. No destination disclosure is required. Access cannot be guaranteed while the bike is away.

The primary mechanism is reducing competing departures through each person's private planning. Calendar scheduling handles the remaining demand. This needs only the calendar, its writing implement, the existing key, and a short shared check. It assumes some outings are flexible and combinable. Longer consolidated outings could occupy the bike across someone else's useful window, and planning could become burdensome; fewer departures alone would not establish success.
EXPAND.experiment:
A volunteer tally owner runs seven days of ordinary calendar reservations followed by seven days with private consolidation added. In both weeks, record bike-related missed intended trips, approximate idle time within the same observation hours, and total coordination minutes. Count separately any intended task abandoned or delayed beyond its useful time because of consolidation; a cancelled request must not silently disappear from the missed-trip count. Destinations stay unrecorded.

Compare matching weekdays and inspect whether longer outings created new conflicts. Stop consolidation if it causes a time-critical trip to be missed or if any adult feels pressured to disclose destinations; continue ordinary reservations. Otherwise, retain it only if missed trips fall without an unacceptable increase in planning effort or delayed tasks, with tolerances agreed beforehand. If requests shrink but missed tasks or conflicts do not, the mechanism has failed. Variable demand limits what two weeks can establish.

EXPAND.title: Improved P0: Reserve only the time you need, with expiring tentative holds
EXPAND.proposal:
Use P0’s first-entry calendar reservations, the strongest fit here because they accommodate irregular trip lengths with little setup. The specific improvement is distinguishing tentative holds from confirmed bookings so uncertain plans do not indefinitely block access.

Agree on one evening confirmation time. Write only initials and departure–return times, including a realistic return buffer. Firm plans are confirmed immediately; uncertain plans receive a question mark and expire at the next confirmation time unless their owner confirms them. Anyone using a tentative hold must confirm it before departure. First confirmed entries stand; overlapping requests require an agreed swap. An expired hold can be claimed without negotiation. Cross out cancellations promptly. Destinations and purposes remain private.

Return the bike and key to agreed places. If late, notify the next adult when reachable through existing means; otherwise update the calendar upon returning. An emergency overrides a booking whenever the bike is home: mark an estimated return and notify displaced users where possible, without requiring an explanation. These resources cannot recall an absent bike.

This changes outcomes by releasing uncertain claims while preserving advance certainty for firm trips. It needs the existing calendar, key, an already available writing implement, and reliable calendar checks. It assumes tentative claims cause some conflicts; there is no evidence yet that they do. If adults cannot maintain confirmation checks, use ordinary P0 immediately: every entered window is a firm commitment, with prompt cancellation.
EXPAND.experiment: One adult volunteers to tally results. Trial ordinary P0 for seven days and the improved version for seven, covering the same weekdays. Each adult records daily trips missed because the bike was unavailable and minutes spent checking or negotiating. Record bike-at-home minutes inside reserved windows as a practical measure of blocked idle time; separately estimate total daylight idle time in half-hour blocks. No destinations are recorded. Count expired holds that actually become completed rides for another adult. Stop the expiry rule if it causes a missed trip through misunderstanding. Retain it only if missed trips or blocked idle time fall without an unacceptable coordination increase. No reclaimed use, unchanged missed trips, or greater effort could show no gain; different weekly demand limits inference.

EXPAND.title: Ration scarce booking time with a weekly hour allowance
EXPAND.proposal:
Give each adult an equal allowance of advance-bookable bike hours. This uses a different lever: a limited entitlement makes holding scarce time consume something the person could use later, encouraging them to reserve only their most useful windows. It differs from awarding conflicts to whoever has ridden least: people choose when to spend their allowance, and past ride counts do not decide priority.

Before starting, agree on the daily hours during which advance bookings need protection. Divide that weekly total equally among the three adults and write each balance on the calendar. A reservation within those hours deducts its duration, including the return buffer. The first affordable entry stands. Cancellation before the preceding evening restores the hours; later cancellation releases the bike but does not restore the allowance. Outside protected hours, or when nobody has reserved it, anyone may borrow the bike without spending allowance, returning before the next booking. Unused allowances expire weekly.

Record only initials, times and balances. Return the key to its agreed place. Emergencies bypass allowances whenever the bike is home; mark the expected return and notify displaced users if reachable. Do not demand destinations or emergency details. A bike already away remains unavailable.

This needs only the calendar, existing key and an available writing implement. It assumes excess advance claims are a meaningful problem and equal booking entitlements are acceptable. Arithmetic, strategic booking and unequal essential needs may outweigh its benefits. If the adults cannot agree on protected hours or allowances before starting, use ordinary P0 for the trial instead. Stop using quotas if an exhausted allowance prevents an otherwise feasible essential reservation; no explanation of the destination is required.
EXPAND.experiment: A volunteer maintains the balances during a bounded two-week comparison: seven days of ordinary P0, followed by seven days with allowances. Use the same protected hours for measurement in both weeks. Each adult tallies bike-unavailable missed trips and daily coordination minutes. Estimate total protected-hours idle time in half-hour blocks and mark reserved portions when the bike remained home. Also count requests refused solely because an allowance was exhausted and disputes about balances. Stop early for an essential reservation refused by the quota or repeated balance disagreements. Lower blocked idle time accompanied by more missed trips is a failure, not a success. If speculative claims are rare, this route may simply add work; weekly demand differences prevent a strong causal conclusion.
